passages: Quick sort is a divide and conquer sorting algorithm. It chooses one element of the array as the pivot and partitions the other elements around it.
In this lab the pivot is the last element of the range, arr[high]. Choosing the last element keeps the partition code short.
The partition function keeps a boundary index i for the region of elements smaller than or equal to the pivot. The index i starts at low - 1, one position before the low boundary.
A second index j scans the range from low to high - 1. When arr[j] <= pivot, i is incremented and arr[i] and arr[j] are swapped.

int partition(int arr[], int low, int high) { int pivot = arr[high]; int i = low - 1; for (int j = low; j < high; j++) { if (arr[j] <= pivot) { i++; swap(arr[i], arr[j]); } } swap(arr[i + 1], arr[high]); return i + 1; }
After the loop, the pivot is swapped into position i + 1. Every element to its left is less than or equal to the pivot and every element to its right is greater.
The recursion stops when low >= high, because a range of zero or one element is already sorted.
Merge sort is also a divide and conquer algorithm. It splits the array at the middle index mid = (low + high) / 2, sorts each half, and merges the two sorted halves.
Merge sort takes O(n log n) time in every case, because the array is halved log n times and each level of merging does O(n) work.
Quick sort takes O(n log n) time on average but O(n^2) in the worst case, when the pivot is always the smallest or largest element.
